source_text: Sunt plane et alia tam stulta, quae pertinent ad contumelias et passiones dei. Aut prudentiam dicant deum crucifixum. Aufer hoc quoque, Mercion, immo hoc potius. Quid enim indignius deo, quid magis erubescendum, nasci an mori? carnem gestare an crucem? eircumcidi an suffigi? educari an sepeliri? in praesepe deponi an in menimento recondi? Sapientior eris si nec ista credideris. Sed non eris sapiens, nisi stultus in saeculo fueris, dei stulta credendo. An ideo passiones a Christo non recidisti, quia ut phantasma vacabat a sensu carum? Diximus retro aeque illum et nativitatis et infantiae imaginariae vacua ludibria subire potuisse. Sed iam hic responde, interfector veritatis, noune vere crucifixus est deus? nonae vere mortuus est, ut vere crucifixus? nonne vere resuscitatus, ut vere scilicet mortuus? Falso se statuit inter nos scire Paulus tantum Iesum crucifixum, falso sepultum ingessit, falso resuscitatum inculcavit. Falsa est igitur et fides nostra, et phantasma erit totum quod speramus a Christo. Scelestissime hominum, qui interemptores excusas dei. Nihil enim ab eis passus est Christus, si nihil vere est passus. Parce unicae spei totius orbis, qui destruis necessarium dedecus fidei. Quodcunque deo indignum est, mihi expedit. Salvus sum si non confundar de domino meo. Qui mei, inquit, confusus fuerit, confundar et ego eius. Alias non invenio materias confusionis quae me per contemptum ruboris probent bene impudentem et feliciter stultum. Crucifixus est dei filius; non pudet, quia pudendum est. Et mortuus est dei filius; prorsus credibile est, quia ineptum est. Et sepultus resurresit; certum est, quia impossibile est. Nam quomodo vera in illo erunt, si ipse non fuit verus, si non vere habuit in se quod figeretur, quod moreretur, quod sepeliretur et resuscitaretur? carnem scilicet hanc sanguine suffusam, ossibus structam, nervis intextam, venia implexam, quae nasci et mori novit, humanam sine dubio, ut natam de homine. Ideoque mortalis haec erit in Christo, quia Christus homo et filius hominis. Aut cur homo Christus et hominis filius, si nihil hominis et nihil ex homine? nisi si aut aliud est homo quam caro, aut aliunde caro hominis quam ex homine, aut aliud est Maria quam homo, aut homo deus Marcionis. Aliter non diceretur homo Christus sine carne, nec hominis filius sine aliquo parente homine, sicut nec deus sine spiritu dei, nec dei filius sine deo patre. Ita utriusque substantiae census hominem et deum exhibuit, hine natum, inde non natum,hinc carneum, inde spiritalem, hine infirmum, inde praefortem, hinc morientem, inde viventem. Quae proprietas conditionum, divinae et humanae, aequa utique naturae cuiusque veritate dispuncta est, eadem fide et spiritus et carnis. Virtutes spiritus dei deum, passiones carnem hominis probaverunt. Si virtutes non sine spiritu, perinde et passiones non sine carne. Si caro cum passionibus ficta, et spiritus ergo cum virtutibus falsus. Quid dimidias mendacio Christum? Totus veritas fuit. Maluit, crede, nasci quam ex aliqua parte mentiri, et quidem in semetipsum, ut carnem gestaret sine ossibus duram, sine musculis solidam, sine sanguine cruentam, sine tunica vestitam, sine fame esurientem, sine dentibus edentem, sine lingua loquentem, ut phantasma auribus fuerit sermo eius per imaginem vocis. Fuit itaque phantasma etiam post resurrectionem, cum manus et pedes suos discipulis inspiciendos offert, Aspicite, dicens quod ego sum quia spiritus ossa non habet, sicut me habentem videtis; sine dubio manus et pedes et ossa, quae spiritus non habet, sed caro. Quomodo hanc vocem interpretaris, Marcion, qui a deo optimo et simplici et bono tantum infers Iesum? Ecce fallit et decipit et circumvenit omnium oculos, omnium sensus, omnium accessus et contactus. Ergo iam Christum non de caelo deferre debueras, sed de aliquo circulatorio coetu, nec deum praeter hominem, sed magum hominem, nec salutis pontificem, sed spectaculi artiflcem, nec mortuorum resuscitatorem, sed vivorum avocatorom Nisi quod et si magus fuit natus est.
thought_title: The Folly of a Crucified and Risen God
orientation: Tertullian is answering Marcion's objection that birth and flesh are unworthy of God, and now turns to the even more shameful things God underwent: death, burial, and crucifixion.
pass_a_gloss: There are plainly also other things so foolish, which pertain to the insults and passions of God. Or let them call a crucified God prudent. Take away this too, Marcion, or rather this more. For what is more unworthy of God, what more to be blushed at, to be born or to die? to carry flesh or a cross? to be circumcised or to be nailed up? to be brought up or to be buried? to be laid in a manger or to be hidden in a tomb? You will be wiser if you will not have believed these things either. But you will not be wise, unless you will have been foolish in the world, by believing the foolish things of God. Or did you not cut away the passions from Christ for this reason, because as a phantom he was free from the sense of flesh? We have said before that he could equally have undergone the empty mockeries of imaginary birth and infancy. But now answer here, killer of truth: was not God truly crucified? was he not truly dead, as truly crucified? was he not truly raised again, as truly of course dead? Falsely did Paul determine to know among us only Jesus crucified, falsely did he press in the buried one, falsely did he inculcate the raised one. False therefore is our faith also, and a phantom will be the whole of what we hope from Christ. Most wicked of men, you who excuse the killers of God. For Christ suffered nothing from them, if he truly suffered nothing. Spare the sole hope of the whole world, you who destroy the necessary shame of faith. Whatever is unworthy of God is expedient for me. I am saved if I am not confounded about my Lord. Whoever, he says, will have been confounded of me, I also will be confounded of him. Elsewhere I do not find materials of confusion which through contempt of shame prove me well shameless and happily foolish. The Son of God was crucified; it is not shameful, because it is shameful. And the Son of God died; it is altogether credible, because it is inept. And buried he rose again; it is certain, because it is impossible. For how will things be true in him, if he himself was not true, if he did not truly have in himself what would be fastened, what would die, what would be buried and raised again? this flesh of course suffused with blood, built with bones, woven with sinews, entwined with veins, which knows how to be born and to die, human without doubt, as born from man. And therefore this will be mortal in Christ, because Christ is man and Son of Man. Or why is Christ man and son of man, if he has nothing of man and nothing from man? Unless if either man is other than flesh, or the flesh of man is from elsewhere than from man, or Mary is other than man, or man is the God of Marcion. Otherwise Christ would not be called man without flesh, nor son of man without some human parent, just as neither God without the spirit of God, nor Son of God without God the Father. Thus the census of each substance exhibited man and God, born from here, not born from there, fleshly from here, spiritual from there, weak from here, very strong from there, dying from here, living from there. Which property of the conditions, divine and human, is equally marked out by the truth of each nature, by the same faith of both spirit and flesh. The powers of the spirit of God proved God, the passions of the flesh proved man. If the powers are not without the spirit, likewise also the passions are not without the flesh. If the flesh with the passions was feigned, then the spirit with the powers was false. Why do you halve Christ with a lie? He was wholly truth. He preferred, believe, to be born than to lie in any part, and indeed in himself, so as to carry flesh hard without bones, solid without muscles, bloody without blood, clothed without a tunic, hungry without hunger, eating without teeth, speaking without a tongue, so that his speech was a phantom to the ears through the image of a voice. Therefore he was a phantom also after the resurrection, when he offers his hands and feet to the disciples to be inspected, saying, Look, because I am, because a spirit does not have bones, as you see me having; without doubt hands and feet and bones, which a spirit does not have, but flesh. How do you interpret this voice, Marcion, who bring in Jesus only from a God best and simple and good? Behold he deceives and tricks and circumvents the eyes of all, the senses of all, the approaches and touches of all. Therefore you should not have brought down Christ from heaven, but from some circus troupe, nor God besides man, but a magician man, nor the priest of salvation, but the artisan of spectacle, nor the raiser of the dead, but the caller away of the living. Unless because even if he was a magician, he was born.

lemmas.gloss: to be nailed up, fastened to a cross

choices.why: Keeps the paradox of God undergoing suffering; 'passions' preserves the Latin passiones and the theological sense of suffering undergone.
Direct address to Marcion; 'killer' is more forceful and literal than 'murderer' and matches interfector.
dedecus means disgrace or shame; 'shame' is the plainest English and matches the following confusionis/ruboris language.
Tertullian's famous paradox credibile quia ineptum; 'inept' preserves the Latin root and the sense of absurdity.
circulatorius refers to itinerant showmen or mountebanks; 'circus troupe' conveys the public spectacle and trickery.
avocator means one who calls away or diverts; 'caller away' keeps the contrast with resuscitatorem (raiser of the dead).

pass_b_english: There are plainly other foolish things too, the ones that belong to the insults and passions of God. Or let them call a crucified God wisdom. Take this away too, Marcion—or rather, take this above all. For what is more unworthy of God, what more shameful: to be born or to die? To carry flesh or a cross? To be circumcised or nailed up? To be brought up or buried? To be laid in a manger or shut in a tomb? You will be wiser if you do not believe these things either. But you will not be wise unless you become a fool in the world by believing God's foolish things. Was it for this reason that you did not cut the passions away from Christ, because as a phantom he lacked any sense of them? We said before that he could equally have undergone the empty mockeries of an imaginary birth and infancy. But answer now, killer of truth: was not God truly crucified? Did he not truly die, because he was truly crucified? Was he not truly raised again, because he truly died? Did Paul falsely set himself to know nothing among us but Jesus crucified (1 Corinthians 2:2)? Did he falsely assert that he was buried, falsely insist that he was raised again (1 Corinthians 15:4)? Then our faith is false too, and everything we hope from Christ will be a phantom. You are the wickedest of men, who excuse the killers of God. For Christ suffered nothing from them if he truly suffered nothing. Spare the one hope of the whole world, you who destroy the necessary shame of faith. Whatever is unworthy of God is for my benefit. I am saved if I am not ashamed of my Lord. Whoever is ashamed of me, he says, I will be ashamed of him too (Mark 8:38). I find no other materials for shame that prove me, through contempt of blushing, well shameless and happily foolish. The Son of God was crucified; I am not ashamed, because it is shameful. And the Son of God died; it is entirely believable, because it is absurd. And he was buried and rose again; it is certain, because it is impossible. For how will these things be true in him if he himself was not true, if he did not truly have in himself what could be fastened, what could die, what could be buried and raised again—this flesh, suffused with blood, built on bones, woven with sinews, entwined with veins, which knows how to be born and to die? Human without doubt, as born from a human. And therefore it will be mortal in Christ, because Christ is man and Son of Man. Or why is Christ man and son of man, if he has nothing of man and nothing from man? Unless either man is something other than flesh, or man's flesh comes from somewhere other than man, or Mary is something other than man, or the God of Marcion is man. Otherwise Christ would not be called man without flesh, nor son of man without some human parent, just as he would not be God without the Spirit of God, nor Son of God without God the Father. Thus the census of both substances exhibited him as man and God: born from here, unborn from there; fleshly from here, spiritual from there; weak from here, supremely strong from there; dying from here, living from there. This property of the conditions, divine and human, is marked out by the equal truth of each nature, by the same faith of both spirit and flesh. The powers of the Spirit of God proved him God; the passions proved the flesh of man. If the powers were not without the Spirit, likewise the passions were not without flesh. If the flesh with its passions was feigned, then the Spirit with its powers was false too. Why do you halve Christ with a lie? He was entirely truth. He preferred, believe me, to be born than to lie in any part—and indeed against himself—by carrying flesh hard without bones, solid without muscles, bloody without blood, clothed without a tunic, hungry without hunger, eating without teeth, speaking without a tongue, so that his speech was a phantom to the ears through the image of a voice. Then he was a phantom even after the resurrection, when he offered his hands and feet to his disciples to inspect, saying, Look, that it is I, for a spirit does not have bones as you see me having (Luke 24:39)—without doubt hands and feet and bones, which a spirit does not have, but flesh does. How do you interpret this voice, Marcion, who bring Jesus only from a God who is best and simple and good? Look, he deceives and tricks and cheats the eyes of all, the senses of all, the approaches and touches of all. Then you should have brought Christ not from heaven but from some circus troupe, not God above man but a man magician, not the high priest of salvation but the artisan of spectacle, not the raiser of the dead but the caller away of the living. Except that even if he was a magician, he was born.

problems.quote: Did Paul falsely determine to know nothing among us but Jesus crucified (1 Corinthians 2:2)?
problems.source_quote: Falso se statuit inter nos scire Paulus tantum Iesum crucifixum
problems.why: Tertullian quotes Paul saying 'I determined to know nothing...' (1 Cor 2:2), but English makes Paul the object of determination ('falsely determine'), flipping agency.
problems.fix: Did Paul falsely set himself to know nothing among us but Jesus crucified (1 Corinthians 2:2)?
problems.ruling: Latin says others claim Paul knows only crucified Jesus; English makes Paul the decision‑maker.

problems.why: 'Ineptum' means absurd/foolish (fitting the paradox pattern: credible because absurd). 'Inept' in modern English means incompetent, wrong sense.
problems.ruling: ‘ineptum’ means absurd/foolish; English ‘inept’ implies incompetence, altering sense.

problems.quote: without bones hard, without muscles solid
problems.source_quote: sine ossibus duram, sine musculis solidam
problems.why: Word order misread: 'duram' and 'solidam' modify 'flesh' (flesh hard without bones, solid without muscles), not the nouns following. English makes bones hard and muscles solid.
problems.fix: flesh hard without bones, solid without muscles
problems.ruling: Adjectives agree with ‘carnem’; translation swaps modifiers, making bones hard.

problems.why: 'Cruentam' modifies flesh (bloody flesh without blood), not 'without blood' as predicate. Same syntactic error as above.
problems.ruling: ‘solidam’ modifies flesh; English makes muscles solid.

problems.why: 'Vestitam' modifies flesh (clothed flesh without tunic), not 'without a tunic'. Same pattern.
problems.ruling: ‘cruentam’ qualifies flesh; English treats as ‘without blood’ predicate.

problems.why: 'Esurientem' modifies flesh (hungry flesh without hunger), not 'without hunger'. Same pattern.
problems.ruling: ‘vestitam’ describes flesh; English mis‑places to tunic.

problems.why: 'Edentem' modifies flesh (eating flesh without teeth), not 'without teeth'. Same pattern.
problems.ruling: ‘esurientem’ qualifies flesh; English renders as ‘without hunger hungry’.

problems.why: 'Loquentem' modifies flesh (speaking flesh without tongue), not 'without a tongue'. Same pattern.
problems.ruling: ‘edentem’, ‘loquentem’ describe flesh; English makes teeth/bones the subjects.

problems.why: Christ's words 'quod ego sum' mean 'that I am' (i.e., that I exist in flesh, not spirit), not 'because I am myself'. Wrong sense of 'quod'.
problems.ruling: ‘quod ego sum’ = ‘that I am’; English adds causal ‘because’.

problems.quote: not God besides man but a magician man
problems.source_quote: nec deum praeter hominem, sed magum hominem
problems.why: 'Praeter hominem' means 'beyond/above man' (i.e., God above man), not 'besides'. Marcion's God is supposed to be purely divine, not God alongside man.
problems.fix: not God above man but a man magician
problems.ruling: ‘praeter hominem’ means ‘beyond/above man’, not ‘besides’; theological nuance altered.

problems.quote: Did Paul falsely determine to know nothing among us but Jesus crucified (1 Corinthians 2:2)? Did he falsely assert that he was buried, falsely insist that he was raised again (1 Corinthians 15:4)?
problems.source_quote: Falso se statuit inter nos scire Paulus tantum Iesum crucifixum, falso sepultum ingessit, falso resuscitatum inculcavit.
problems.why: Latin says Marcion falsely claims Paul taught that Jesus was only crucified, buried, and resurrected; English makes Paul the one who falsely taught, reversing agency.
problems.fix: Marcion falsely claims that Paul taught only that Jesus was crucified, that he was buried, and that he was resurrected.
problems.ruling: Latin 'Falso se statuit...Paulus' = Marcion falsely claimed Paul taught this; English 'Did Paul falsely determine' reverses agency to Paul himself.

fixed: Fixed: 'Falso se statuit inter nos scire Paulus' means Paul set himself to know, so 'set himself' is correct.
Fixed: 'ineptum' here means absurd/foolish, not incompetent.
Fixed: 'duram' and 'solidam' modify 'carnem' (flesh), not the nouns following.
Fixed: 'quod ego sum' means 'that I am', not 'because I am myself'.

problems.quote: it is not shameful, because it is shameful
problems.why: "non pudet" means "I am not ashamed" (impersonal verb). The English says the thing is "not shameful", which contradicts "because it is shameful" and loses Tertullian's paradox.
problems.fix: The Son of God was crucified; I am not ashamed, because it is shameful.

problems.quote: Did you spare Christ the passions because as a phantom he was free from the sense of them?
problems.source_quote: An ideo passiones a Christo non recidisti, quia ut phantasma vacabat a sensu carum?
problems.why: Latin asks why he did not cut the passions away; English asks whether he exempted Christ from them.
problems.fix: Was it for this that you did not cut the passions away from Christ, because as a phantom he lacked any sense of them?
problems.ruling: Source 'passiones a Christo non recidisti' = did you not cut the passions from Christ; English 'spare Christ the passions' inverts the negated verb and meaning.

problems.why: educari means to be brought up. Raised reads as resurrection, the opposite pole of this shame contrast.
problems.fix: To be brought up or buried?
problems.ruling: 'educari an sepeliri' = be brought up/nurtured vs buried; 'raised' invites resurrection reading, contradicting the birth-to-death shame contrast.

problems.quote: he carried flesh flesh hard without bones
problems.source_quote: ut carnem gestaret sine ossibus duram
problems.why: Flesh is doubled, so the phrase does not parse.
problems.fix: so as to carry flesh hard without bones
problems.ruling: 'carnem gestaret sine ossibus duram': English 'carried flesh flesh hard' has a duplicated word; garbled and unreadable, though meaning recoverable.

fixed: non pudet, quia pudendum est: changed impersonal thing-judgment to first-person I am not ashamed to restore paradox.
non recidisti: restored missing negation as did not cut the passions away from Christ.
educari an sepeliri: changed raised to brought up, since educari is upbringing not resurrection.
ut carnem gestaret sine ossibus duram: deleted doubled flesh to read flesh hard without bones.

problems.quote: He preferred, believe me, to be born than to lie in any part—and indeed against himself—so that he carried flesh hard without bones
problems.source_quote: Maluit, crede, nasci quam ex aliqua parte mentiri, et quidem in semetipsum, ut carnem gestaret sine ossibus duram
problems.why: The purpose clause is attached to being born. In the source it belongs to the lie: Marcion's Christ would carry boneless phantom flesh. The English makes birth the means of carrying that flesh, which is nonsense.
problems.fix: He preferred, believe me, to be born rather than to lie in any part, and against himself at that, by carrying flesh hard without bones, solid without muscles...

problems.quote: he deceives and tricks and circumvents the eyes of all, the senses of all, the approaches and touches of all
problems.source_quote: fallit et decipit et circumvenit omnium oculos, omnium sensus, omnium accessus et contactus
problems.why: circumvenit means he cheats every sight, sense, approach, and touch, not that he evades them.
problems.fix: he deceives, tricks, and cheats the eyes of all, the senses of all, and every approach and touch
problems.ruling: "fallit et decipit et circumvenit" — all three mean deceive/cheat; "circumvents" in English suggests evading, misleading reader; meaning is he deceives the eyes and senses.

last_rejected.fix: so that he carried flesh hard, without bones,
last_rejected.ruling: Latin: "carnem ... sine ossibus duram" = hard flesh without bones; English phrasing conveys same.

last_rejected.why: The adjective 'cruentam' (bloody) modifies 'carnem' (flesh), not 'sanguine' (blood). The English incorrectly attaches 'bloody' to the blood.
last_rejected.ruling: Latin: "sine sanguine cruentam" = bloody flesh without blood; English matches.

last_rejected.why: The participle 'esurientem' (hungry) modifies 'carnem' (flesh), not 'fame' (hunger). The English incorrectly attaches 'hungry' to the hunger.
last_rejected.ruling: Latin: "sine fame esurientem" = hungry flesh without hunger; English matches.

last_rejected.why: The participle 'edentem' (eating) modifies 'carnem' (flesh), not 'dentibus' (teeth). The English incorrectly attaches 'eating' to the teeth.
last_rejected.ruling: Latin: "sine dentibus edentem" = eating flesh without teeth; English matches.

last_rejected.why: The participle 'loquentem' (speaking) modifies 'carnem' (flesh), not 'lingua' (tongue). The English incorrectly attaches 'speaking' to the tongue.
last_rejected.ruling: Latin: "sine lingua loquentem" = speaking flesh without a tongue; English matches.
